Readable C export
=================

Cesta writes its constructs as ordinary C that a project commits and builds
with GCC or Clang alone. There are two routes, sharing one checked lowering.

  cesta export-c [--cc COMPILER] [--plan PLAN] [-o OUTPUT.c] INPUT.cesta [-- FLAGS]
  cesta export-header [--plan PLAN] EXPORT-SPEC -o OUTPUT.h

Program export
--------------

export-c writes a whole Cesta unit as C. Each macro use stays where it is, as
a statement expression: every evaluated argument is acquired once, in
declared order, into a named local, and its declared type is checked exactly
on that local, so argument text is never repeated:

  return ({
    __auto_type value_1 = value;
    _Static_assert(_Generic(value_1, uint64_t: 1, default: 0), "...");
    __auto_type out_1 = out;
    _Static_assert(_Generic(out_1, uint32_t *: 1, default: 0), "...");
    ({
      uint32_t converted;
      int accepted = 0;
      ...
      accepted;
    });
  });

Template locals keep their module names. A name is suffixed only where it
would shadow a name the unit writes or a native macro mentions. The output
has the same objects as compiling the unit through cesta cc.

Program export keeps the in-place form for arguments it cannot acquire once
without changing meaning: deferred and repeated arguments, statement macros
of the c11 profile, and arguments that would be copied while naming
__COUNTER__, __LINE__ or a macro defined with them. Those uses are refused
with a pointer to cesta expand, which keeps the exact form.

--plan records each use as a cesta-export-plan/2 record: the rule, the
arguments as written, the names chosen for acquisitions and locals in the
order they were chosen, the position, and the structure handed to the
printer, with every argument in place.

Library export
--------------

export-header reads a cesta-export/1 specification and writes one header of
named C definitions:

  (cesta-export/1
    (header CT_SIZES_H)
    (profile gnu11)
    (include <stdint.h>)
    (include "pair.h")
    (use "Sizes.module" Checked)
    (function ct_pair_bytes_u32 ArrayBytes (element Pair) (count uint32_t) (size size_t)
      (doc "..."))
    (macro ct_probe Probe (doc "...")))

function makes one static inline function per concrete instance; every type
parameter is named in the specification. A construct qualifies when each
evaluated argument is acquired once and the template has no caller context:
no captures, native definition ports, return, break, continue, goto or
__func__. Places become pointer parameters.

A C call evaluates its arguments once each, in an order C leaves
unspecified, and its prototype converts arguments to the parameter types.
That is the header's contract. Callers that need ordered effects sequence
them; callers that need exact types use program export.

macro makes a function-like macro for constructs whose parameters all take
syntax, such as probes. Evaluated parameters are refused: textual substitution
does not capture their values or places once. Use a function or keep the
in-place expansion for those constructs. A macro is one parenthesized
expression, safe under if and else, and its
static assertions sit inside sizeof so the macro needs no statement wrapper.

Parameter and local names are protected from macros the includer defines,
with push_macro and pop_macro around the definitions. Exported names and
required compiler builtins are checked at the top of the header.

Counter tables
--------------

A counter table is structured data, not C text:

  (cesta-counters/1
    (enum CettaRuntimeCounter)
    (prefix CETTA_RUNTIME_COUNTER_)
    (count COUNT)
    (names CETTA_RUNTIME_COUNTER_NAMES)
    (profile dense)
    (rows
      (0 BINDINGS_LOOKUP "bindings-lookup")
      (1 BINDINGS_CLONE "bindings-clone")))

(counters FILE) in a specification emits the enumeration and its count;
(counter-names FILE) emits the spelling array, for the one source file that
defines it. The dense profile requires IDs 0 to n-1 in order, unique names
and spellings, C identifiers, and printable spellings without quotes or
backslashes.

Evidence
--------

Program export produces objects identical to cesta cc for every library, on
both compilers, unoptimized and optimized. Exported headers compile
standalone under -pedantic -Werror, behave as the library tests require, and
keep their meaning when the includer defines macros with their local names.
A counter table exported from CeTTa's runtime counters gives objects
identical to CeTTa's own definitions, and the Lean kernel decides that its
actual rows have the dense profile (ExportCounterTables.Dense).

Program export is proved against a model of the C it writes, in MeTTapedia's
MacroExport modules. There the lowering is restated as a function of the rule
and the arguments as written. For every recorded use, the Lean kernel decides
that the recorded structure is exactly that lowering, that the rule lies in
the fragment the proof covers, and that the chosen names are distinct.
recorded_export_correct then states: the recorded block, run by an interpreter
for the C fragment the templates use, has the outcome of the source use from
any state, with any caller code and any replies from called functions. That is
the same value or fault, the same memory, the same ordered calls, the same
replies consumed and the same private frame. Compound-assignment inputs and
unsequenced operands are checked as simple reads. A plain assignment to a
named local may have an effectful right operand because its left operand
only designates a location. These checks make the selected evaluation order
unobservable in the admitted fragment.

The check is complete for the forms the exporter lowers, so what it accepts
is not limited to the recorded uses. A rule is in those forms when it uses
the gnu11 profile, evaluates each evaluated argument once and gives it a C
type, and gives an expression's result a C type. Outside them the exporter
refuses the use, and a module whose rule lacks those types does not load.
export_complete states: for such a rule, arguments of the
right number and any supply of enough distinct names, a prefix of the supply
is exactly the names the lowering uses, the block fills in the arguments as
written, its record is admitted, and the block behaves as the use. The kernel
decides that every recorded rule, the shipped ones included, is in these
forms.

The library contracts are proved on the rules the modules ship:
  - try-narrow and array-bytes store a representable result and otherwise
    keep the destination;
  - doubled-capacity starts at the initial value, doubles, or refuses an
    overflow and keeps the destination;
  - worklist-push refuses aliased, overfull and unallocated arguments with no
    effect, and appends when there is room. When the buffer is full it makes
    exactly one resize call. If the new size overflows it refuses before
    calling, and if the resize returns null it refuses and keeps the buffer;
  - a disabled probe runs nothing and an enabled one runs its effect once.

Not proved:
  - that GCC and Clang give the interpreted fragment the meaning the
    interpreter gives it;
  - that the printed C reads back as the recorded structure;
  - what the caller's code and a resize function do, which the laws take as
    hypotheses;
  - that the counter rows read from CeTTa's sources are the rows CeTTa
    compiles, which identical objects test.
The first two are tested: the export gives objects identical to cesta cc and
is compiled and run with both compilers, and the kernel refuses recorded
blocks mutated in their stores, guards, branches, intrinsics, callees,
acquisition order, duplicated acquisitions, scopes, result checks and names.
Chosen names are checked against the written arguments for capture.

Header export is proved the same way. export-header --plan records each
definition: the rule, the type parameters, the names chosen, and the
definition handed to the printer (for a macro, its expression before it
becomes text). The kernel decides that every shipped header definition is the
lowering of its rule. function_correct states that a function's body, run with
its parameters holding the values and places a call supplies, has the outcome
of the rule's template with those arguments. That gives each shipped header
function its library's contract, and the probe macro, at a use, runs its
effect exactly when its switch is nonzero. Header export is complete in the
same sense: every function of a rule whose parameter declarators each have
one slot and whose expression result is a plain C type, and every macro of a
rule with syntax parameters only and no locals whose template is not empty,
and not a block when the
rule is an expression, is admitted for any distinct names
(checkHeader_function_complete, checkHeader_macro_complete).

A header's promise stops at the call. C evaluates the call's arguments in an
unspecified order and converts them to the parameter types: a call with two
effectful arguments can run them in either order, and a prototype converts
what the exact contract refuses. Callers that need ordered effects or exact
types use program export.

Tests
-----

make check runs bounded local checks, make test the regression suite, and
make qualify every gate, including corpora and Lean. A project consuming an
exported header runs none of them.
